There are tons of different benchmarks that they can use to claim something is "faster".

for example: How long does it wait to begin rendering the page after the contents have started transmitting?

One way you could implement a browser, you start rendering the page immediately, Sure, layouts will change a little bit, and you will have to re-render a few times, but to the user, it looks like your browser responded 100% faster than in another browser

Another, you wait until the page has completely loaded, or mostly loaded, before rendering. The page may not immediately render, but once it is loaded, it renders exactly one time, and doesn't have to keep loading content and re-sizing itself. Therefore, it rendered much quicker, which gives the visual appearance that the browser is much faster than the other browser (despite taking a little longer to respond)

Each browser could say it was faster than the other in the case above. There's also so many different parts of the browser. One browser may have a faster javascript engine, the other faster css rendering. faster processing of a specific filetype. A browser manufacturer can study a javascript benchmark, and improve speed related to those benchmarks (and simultaneously reduce performance in other areas). Then, they could use that benchmark to say they are faster than the other browser.
